implementation_notes: Resilience4j is the Java default: CircuitBreaker.of(name, config) builds a thread-safe state machine (state in an AtomicReference, recording and snapshots synchronized, the protected call deliberately outside the critical section) and decorateSupplier, executeSupplier, decorateCheckedSupplier or executeCompletionStage wrap the dependency call. CircuitBreakerConfig sets failureRateThreshold, slowCallRateThreshold, minimumNumberOfCalls, slidingWindowType/slidingWindowSize, waitDurationInOpenState, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState and the classification knobs recordExceptions, ignoreExceptions and recordFailurePredicate, while the registry guarantees one named instance per dependency. While open it throws CallNotPermittedException, and events (state transition, success, recorded error, ignored error) drive metrics. The classic hand-written form is justified only where no dependency may be added; note that Resilience4j 3 requires Java 21 at runtime even though the API style is Java 8 era.
code_sketch:
CircuitBreaker payments = CircuitBreaker.of("payments", CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
    .failureRateThreshold(50)
    .minimumNumberOfCalls(20)
    .slidingWindowType(SlidingWindowType.TIME_BASED)
    .slidingWindowSize(30)                              // seconds
    .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(15))
    .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(3)
    .recordExceptions(IOException.class, TimeoutException.class)
    .ignoreExceptions(DeclinedException.class)           // business error, never trips
    .build());

Receipt r = payments.executeSupplier(() -> api.authorize(order));
// open -> CallNotPermittedException: map to the fallback, do not retry
pitfalls: CallNotPermittedException must be mapped explicitly; a generic retry template that retries RuntimeException keeps hammering an open circuit.
Use one instance per dependency: the default registry configuration is shared, so an ofDefaults instance reused across services merges failure domains.
The sliding window counts concurrent calls but does not limit them; the window size is not a concurrency limit, so pair it with a Bulkhead for that purpose.
METRICS_ONLY, DISABLED and FORCED_OPEN are sticky special states: a breaker forced open by an operator stays open until it is reset, which surprises automated tests.
Resilience4j 3 requires Java 21 at runtime, so the version you pin decides the minimum runtime even though the configuration API itself looks unchanged.

variants.name: Declarative breaker: annotation or factory around the call
variants.idiom_name: CircuitBreaker annotation / CircuitBreakerFactory (Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker)
variants.implementation_notes: The declarative realization keeps the breaker out of the method body: an annotation such as CircuitBreaker(name = "payments", fallbackMethod = "cachedReceipt") on the service method, or Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker's CircuitBreakerFactory/ReactiveCircuitBreaker around a code block, turns the call into a proxied invocation whose settings live in configuration and whose fallback is a sibling method. Choose it when the dependency call sits in an application service and AOP is already in the stack, because the policy is then applied consistently and reviewable in one place; keep the programmatic variant for infrastructure code, for lambdas that are not beans, and when the breaker must be composed dynamically with retry and time limiter. Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker ships several implementations (Resilience4J, Spring Retry, Spring Framework Retry) behind the same facade, so the semantics you get depend on which one is on the classpath.
pitfalls: Self-invocation bypasses the proxy, so calling the annotated method from another method of the same bean never goes through the breaker.
The fallback signature must match the annotated method plus the throwable, and it must not call the same dependency (or take a lock) or the degradation path becomes the outage.
Configuration lives in properties or YAML, so thresholds can differ between environments and are invisible in the call site's review.
The facade hides different implementations with different semantics (Spring Retry versus Resilience4J), and documentation copied across them produces wrong thresholds.
